newsitem.title: DENMARK: Analysts fret over lower Danish 1997 c/a prospects.
newsitem.headline: Analysts fret over lower Danish 1997 c/a prospects.

text.p: Bank analysts expressed concern on Wednesday about the deteriorating Danish current account and the prospects of a lower than expected 1997 surplus.

"We are now a bit more concerned about the current account trend than previously and we could soon to have raise the alarm," economist Per Hviid at Denmark's biggest bank Den Danske Bank told Reuters.
"The 1997 current account surplus could fall to around five billion crowns," he said.
Earlier the Danish Statistics Office released data showing that May's current account surplus was 0.3 billion crowns, compared to balance in April and a 1.83 billion crown surplus in May 1996.
A panel of analysts polled by Reuters had forecast an average 1.2 billion crown current account surplus in May.
The latest data brought Denmark's current account surplus for the first five months of 1997 to a combined 3.6 billion crowns, against 13.0 billion crowns for the same 1996 period.
Den Danske Bank in June forecast a Danish current account surplus of 14.8 billion crowns for full year 1997, compared to last year's 16.7 billion crown surplus.
The statistics office on Wednesday upwardly revised 1996's full year current account surplus by 1.9 billion crowns to 16.7 billion crowns.

Hviid said that growing imports of consumer goods were the main cause of the deterioration in Denmark's current account and recommended that the government consider action to curb domestic consumption.
Economists have pointed to the housing market as an area where the government could move in to curb demand.
Hviid said his fears about the 1997 current account did not change his expectations for an improvement in 1998, dependent on the extent demand grew in Germany, France and Sweden.

"The latest data were not specially positive. It does not look like we are going to see a current account surplus of over 10 billion crowns this year," senior analyst Jesper Nielsen, at second biggest bank Unidanmark said.
He said he did not expect Danish industrial exports to take off until German demand bucked up, forecasting also that Denmark's imports of private consumer items would stay at the present high level.
